description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of the Psalms. v1.0.0 (2026-11-01, Editor pass, claude-opus-5-5, Writings wave W1: Pss 8, 19, 33, 139, 147) creates the overlay. It holds the ten shared Writings conventions, identical in text and appliesTo in the job-woh, psalms-woh, proverbs-woh and ecclesiastes-woh overlays (English proper names; divine names and the Elohim article; the šāmayim register application; ʾereṣ 'earth' / 'land'; the ʾādām / ben-ʾādām / ʾĕnôš terms; nepeš scope; rûaḥ 'wind' / 'breath' / 'spirit'; Ketiv/Qere; MT baseline, versification and Psalm numbering; poetic lineation and speech marking). Shared entries must be extended in all four overlays together. Candidates for promotion to central: the ʾereṣ cosmic-scope clause (now applied by isaiah-woh and the Writings) and the divine-names article rule. Psalms-specific entries: the superscription terms, the six Torah terms of Ps 19:8-10, and tĕsukkēnî 'you knit me together' (Ps 139:13). Signed off at human review on 2026-11-01 (zarazinsfuss); this wave's central proposals were applied as central glossary v2.87.0, and the sign-off merge is v2.90.0.

entries.source: דָּוִד / שְׁלֹמֹה / יְרוּשָׁלִַם / יִשְׂרָאֵל / יַעֲקֹב / צִיּוֹן / אִיּוֹב

entries.lemma: personal names and toponyms in Job, Psalms, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes
entries.standardEnglish: ASV English forms (David, Solomon, Jerusalem, Israel, Jacob, Zion, Job)
entries.wohChoice: English forms for personal names and toponyms in the Writings, as in the signed-off job-woh chapters and the ezekiel-woh overlay: David (Ps 8:1; 19:1; 139:1), Solomon (Prov 10:1), Jerusalem and Zion (Ps 147:2, 12), Israel and Jacob (Ps 147:2, 19), Job (Job 37:14). Divine names follow divine-names-convention-writings.
entries.rationale: The corpus has two practices for names. job-woh (signed off 2026-05: 'Job', 'Uz') and ezekiel-woh (proper-names-english-forms-convention-ezekiel) use English forms; the Kings overlays transliterate under founder decision A (Yisra'el, Yerushalayim, Shelomoh). The four Writings books follow the job-woh practice. Job-woh is the nearest precedent for the poetic books, and Job 37 must match the stable chapters of its own book, which are not retro-edited. A single practice must also hold across the wave, so that Ps 147 and Job 37 do not differ. Solomon is 'Shelomoh' in 1 Kings woh; the difference is recorded here for the corpus-wide alignment decision that the ezekiel-woh overlay already flagged. The entry carries no lens: name forms are typographical conventions, and the Hebrew form of every name stands in the source text.

entries.source: יְהוָה / יָהּ / אֱלֹהִים / הָאֱלֹהִים / אֵל / אֱלוֹהַּ / שַׁדַּי / אֲדֹנֵינוּ
entries.translit: YHWH / yāh / ʾĕlōhîm / hāʾĕlōhîm / ʾēl / ʾĕlôah / šadday / ʾădōnênû
entries.lemma: the divine names and titles of the Writings
entries.partOfSpeech: proper nouns and titles - book-wide rendering convention
entries.literal: YHWH / Yah / Elohim / the Elohim / El / Eloah / Shaddai / our lord
entries.standardEnglish: Jehovah / Jehovah (in 'Praise ye Jehovah') / God / God / God / God / the Almighty / our Lord (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'YHWH' for the Tetragrammaton. 'Yah' for the short form, so hallĕlû-yāh is 'Praise Yah!' (Ps 147:1, 20). ʾĕlōhîm untranslated (central elohim-as-translation), with the English article only where the Hebrew has it: 'the Elohim' for hāʾĕlōhîm (Eccl 3:11, 14, 15, 17, 18), 'Elohim' for anarthrous ʾĕlōhîm (Ps 8:6; Eccl 3:10, 13), 'our / your / whose Elohim' for suffixed forms (Ps 33:12; 147:1, 7, 12); verbs and pronouns singular where the Hebrew is singular. ʾēl 'El', ʾĕlôah 'Eloah' and šadday 'Shaddai' transliterated as in job-woh (central shaddai-eloah, extended in wave W1): Job 37:5, 10, 14, 15, 22, 23; Ps 19:2; 139:17, 19, 23. The title ʾădōnênû 'our Lord' (Ps 8:2, 10; 147:5), kept distinct from YHWH.
entries.rationale: The corpus keeps the Hebrew divine names visible instead of replacing them with 'God', 'the LORD' and 'the Almighty' (central elohim-as-translation and shaddai-eloah; the isaiah-woh overlay's distinction between 'YHWH' and 'the Lord'). Three points needed a ruling for the Writings. (1) The article. The central entry adds 'the' in narrative so that 'Elohim' reads as a plural class noun; it was written for Genesis 1. Ecclesiastes alternates anarthrous ʾĕlōhîm and articular hāʾĕlōhîm within one chapter (3:10, 13 against 3:11, 14, 15, 17, 18), and Ps 8:6 has anarthrous mēʾĕlōhîm. Following the Hebrew article keeps that variation visible, as the Kings overlay does for anarthrous predicate and genitive ʾĕlōhîm (elohim-referent-and-article-conventions-kings, clause 2) and job-woh does at Job 1:9 ('fear Elohim') against 2:10 ('from the Elohim'). At Ps 8:6 the canon quotes 'the Elohim' with the article; the line follows the Hebrew, and the difference is stated in the reception note. (2) El, Eloah and Shaddai. Job's dialogues use these names, and job-woh transliterates them (38:41; 40:2, 9). Ps 19:2 (kĕbôd-ʾēl), 139:17, 23 (ʾēl) and 139:19 (ʾĕlôah) use the same poetic names, and the same practice is extended to them through a wave-W1 modification of central shaddai-eloah. The isaiah-woh overlay translates these words 'God' in Second Isaiah's denial formulas, where the three words alternate inside one argument; no such formula occurs in this wave. (3) Yah. The short name occurs in the formula hallĕlû-yāh (Ps 147:1, 20). 'Hallelujah' turns the name into a liturgical word, and 'Praise the LORD' or the ASV 'Praise ye Jehovah' replaces it; 'Praise Yah' keeps both the imperative and the name. 'Lord' for ʾădōnênû follows the ASV and the isaiah-woh 'the Lord'.

entries.wohChoice: The central shamayim register rule applied in the Writings. 'skies' where šāmayim is the physical sky, including the sky of creation and the sky seen by day and night (Ps 8:2, 4, 9; 19:2, 7; 33:6; 147:8; Prov 8:27; Eccl 3:1 'under the skies'; Job 37:3). 'heavens' where it is the dwelling of YHWH or the height of the cosmos set against She'ol (Ps 33:13, parallel to 'the place of his dwelling'; 139:8). šĕḥāqîm, the poetic partner of šāmayim, is 'clouds' (central shechaqim-clouds-cross-corpus), never 'skies'.
entries.rationale: The central entry renders šāmayim 'skies' and lets the rendering scale with register. The founder's ruling at the Kings wave-A sign-off (2026-11-01) fixed the test: the physical sky is 'skies', the realm or dwelling of YHWH is 'heaven(s)'. The poetic books use both senses, often in neighbouring lines, so the test is applied verse by verse. The created sky of the creation hymns (Ps 33:6; Prov 8:27) and the sky that shows the moon, the stars, the sun, the clouds and the birds (Ps 8:4, 9; 19:2, 7; 147:8) are physical. In Ps 8:2 the splendor is set upon the same sky that the speaker sees in v 4. Ps 33:13 is the place from which YHWH looks down, glossed in v 14 as 'the place of his dwelling', the sense in which 1 Kgs 8:30, 39 has 'heavens'. Ps 139:8 sets šāmayim against She'ol as the upper extreme of the cosmos (cf. Amos 9:2) and has 'heavens', like Elijah's ascent at 2 Kgs 2:1, 11. Eccl 3:1 taḥat haššāmayim is Qohelet's variant of 'under the sun' and names the visible world. This entry records the site-by-site application; it does not change the central rule.

entries.standardEnglish: earth (ASV, at the cosmic and hymnic sites); land (territorial sites)
entries.wohChoice: 'earth' where ʾereṣ is the whole world or the ground under the sky: the universal formulas kol-hāʾāreṣ 'all the earth' and yōšĕbê hāʾāreṣ 'the inhabitants of the earth' (Ps 8:2, 10; 19:5; 33:5, 8, 14); ʾereṣ parallel to tēbēl 'world' or to šāmayim in creation (Prov 8:23, 26, 29, 31; Job 37:12); the ground on which snow and rain fall or toward which the breath of beasts goes down (Job 37:6, 17; Ps 147:8, 15; Eccl 3:21); the depths of the earth (Ps 139:15). 'ground' for ʿădê-ʾāreṣ 'down to the ground' (Ps 147:6). The central eretz default 'land' governs where ʾereṣ is territory or settled land (Prov 10:30 'dwell in the land'; Job 37:13 'his land'), and kanpôt hāʾāreṣ 'the wings of the land' (Job 37:3) follows job-woh 38:13.
entries.rationale: The central eretz entry fixes 'land' as the default; it was written for Gen 1, where ʾereṣ is paired with šāmayim in a local, physical setting, and it has one context clause ('ground', Ezekiel). The poetic books use ʾereṣ mostly in a universal register: parallel to tēbēl 'world' (Ps 19:5; 33:8; Prov 8:26, 31; Job 37:12) and in the hymnic formula 'all the earth', which the ASV, NRSV and NJPS all render 'earth'. The default 'land' would make Ps 8:2 read 'how majestic is your name in all the land', a territorial claim the Hebrew does not make. The isaiah-woh overlay ruled the same way for the cosmic register of Isa 24 and 40-66 (eretz-cosmic-scope-isaiah-24), and this entry adopts that ruling for the Writings. With two books now applying it, the clause is a candidate for promotion to the central eretz entry. 'Land' is kept where ʾereṣ names settled territory (Prov 10:30; cf. 2:21-22) or 'his land' (Job 37:13), and the stable job-woh phrase 'the wings of the land' (38:13) is reused at Job 37:3. The choice of English word does not decide any question about the planet; it follows the scope of the Hebrew in each verse (BDB ʾereṣ 1-3; HALOT).

entries.source: אָדָם / הָאָדָם / בֶּן־אָדָם / בְּנֵי אָדָם / בְּנֵי הָאָדָם / אֱנוֹשׁ / אִישִׁים / אֲנָשִׁים
entries.translit: ʾādām / hāʾādām / ben-ʾādām / bĕnê ʾādām / bĕnê hāʾādām / ʾĕnôš / ʾîšîm / ʾănāšîm
entries.lemma: the words for human beings in the Writings
entries.literal: human / son(s) of human / mortal / men
entries.standardEnglish: man / the son of man / the sons of men / men (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: hāʾādām and ʾādām 'the human' / 'every human' (central ha-adam: Job 37:7; Prov 8:34; Eccl 3:11, 13, 19, 22). bĕnê hāʾādām 'the sons of the human' (central ha-adam, as genesis-woh at Gen 11:5: Ps 33:13; Eccl 3:10, 18, 19, 21). ben-ʾādām 'a son of human' and anarthrous bĕnê ʾādām 'the sons of human' (central ben-adam: Ps 8:5; Prov 8:4, 31). ʾĕnôš 'a mortal' (Ps 8:5). ʾîšîm 'O men' (Prov 8:4); ʾîš and ʾănāšîm 'a man', 'men' (Job 37:20, 24; Ps 147:10).
entries.rationale: The corpus renders ʾādām as a category noun, 'the human' (central ha-adam, direct), and ben-ʾādām as 'son of human' (central ben-adam, direct, whose rationale already cites Ps 8:5). The plural construct bĕnê (hā)ʾādām is the same decision in the plural. genesis-woh renders it 'the sons of the human' at Gen 11:5 under ha-adam, and this entry follows that precedent. The article follows the Hebrew: 'the sons of the human' for bĕnê hāʾādām, 'the sons of human' for anarthrous bĕnê ʾādām (Prov 8:4, 31), where the English article on 'sons' is needed by English, not by the Hebrew. One English word for one Hebrew word lets Eccl 3:18-21 keep its argument visible ('the sons of the human ... the human has no advantage over the beast'), which the ASV mixture of 'sons of men' and 'man' obscures. The ASV 'sons of men' and the 1 Kgs 8:39 woh 'the children of men' are recorded; the Kings line is the corpus outlier and is flagged for alignment in the wave-W1 editor report. ʾĕnôš (BDB 'man, mankind', often with a note of frailty) is 'a mortal', to keep it distinct from ʾādām in Ps 8:5. The gendered nouns ʾîš and ʾănāšîm keep 'man' and 'men'.

entries.wohChoice: 'life' where nepeš is the life that is saved from death or lost (Ps 33:19 'to deliver their life from death'; Prov 8:36 'wrongs his own life', set against 'life' and 'death' in vv 35-36), as in the Kings and Ezekiel overlays. 'soul' (ASV) where nepeš is the self that is restored, waits, knows or hungers (Ps 19:8; 33:20; 139:14; Prov 10:3). No transliteration in these books.
entries.rationale: nepeš covers throat, appetite, breath, life, person and self (BDB; HALOT; Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 1974). The Kings overlays (nefesh-scope-and-spelling-kings) and the Ezekiel overlay (nefesh-scope-ezekiel) render it 'life' where a life is saved or forfeited, because the ASV 'soul' suggests the later doctrine of an immortal soul, which those passages do not address. The same reasoning applies at Ps 33:19, where 'deliver ... from death' is parallel to 'keep them alive in famine', and at Prov 8:36, which closes the antithesis 'whoever finds me has found life ... all who hate me love death'. In the language of prayer nepeš is the self as the subject of feeling and knowing ('our nepeš waits for YHWH', Ps 33:20; 'my nepeš knows it very well', 139:14) and the self restored by the law (19:8); there the ASV 'soul' is the established English and is kept. Prov 10:3 uses nepeš for the appetite in an image of hunger; 'soul' is kept and the sense is given in commentary, since the alternatives either drop the noun (NRSV 'the righteous') or overtranslate it ('throat'). The Kings transliteration 'nefesh' is reserved for passages that name the nepeš as the life that departs or returns; none occurs in this wave.

entries.wohChoice: 'wind' for the meteorological rûaḥ (Job 37:21; Ps 147:18 'he makes his wind blow'). 'breath' for the breath of the mouth that carries speech (Ps 33:6 'the breath of his mouth') and for the life-breath shared by humans and beasts (Eccl 3:19, 21, one rendering in both verses). Lower-case 'spirit' for YHWH's own rûaḥ as presence (Ps 139:7 'your spirit', parallel to 'your presence'). No capital 'Spirit'; the Kings and Ezekiel transliteration 'ruach' is not used in these books.
entries.rationale: rûaḥ covers wind, breath and spirit (BDB; HALOT), and English must choose. The Writings follow the isaiah-woh overlay (ruach-divine-spirit-lower-case-isaiah), not the Kings and Ezekiel transliteration, which is reserved for narrative passages where the rûaḥ acts as an agent that lifts or carries a prophet. In the poetic books rûaḥ is parallel to 'word' (Ps 33:6), to 'presence' (Ps 139:7) or to the breath of every living thing (Eccl 3:19), and an English word gives the sense without loss. YHWH's rûaḥ at Ps 139:7 is lower-case 'spirit', as in NRSV and NJPS; the ASV capital brings in the later doctrine of a personal Holy Spirit. In Eccl 3:19-21 the ASV has 'breath' in v 19 and 'spirit' in v 21, so one Hebrew word gets two English words inside one argument, and the English seems to separate what humans and beasts share (v 19) from what might rise (v 21). The Hebrew draws no such line: the question of v 21 concerns the same rûaḥ that v 19 says all have alike (cf. Gen 6:17; 7:15, 22; Ps 104:29-30). 'Breath' in both verses keeps the argument visible (NJPS 'lifebreath' at v 21; BDB rûaḥ 2, 'breath of life'). The entry is classed inferred because the traditional English of v 21 is 'spirit'. Eccl 12:7 ('the rûaḥ returns to the Elohim who gave it') should be checked against this entry when the book is extended.

entries.lemma: Ketiv ('what is written', the consonantal text) and Qere ('what is read', the Masoretic reading tradition)
entries.literal: the written consonants vs the vocalized reading
entries.standardEnglish: the ASV and the major English versions translate the Qere, with exceptions (the ASV follows the Ketiv at Ps 139:16 and 147:19)
entries.wohChoice: Translate the Qere and record the Ketiv in commentary at every site. Wave W1 (6 pairs): Job 37:12 (K btḥbwltw, singular / Q bĕtaḥbûlōtāyw, plural, 'by his guidance'); Ps 139:6 (K plʾyh / Q pĕlîʾâ 'wonderful', orthographic); Ps 139:16 (K wlʾ 'and not' / Q wĕlô 'and to it'; the ASV follows the Ketiv); Ps 147:19 (K dbrw 'his word' / Q dĕbārāyw 'his words'; the ASV follows the Ketiv); Prov 8:17 (K ʾhbyh 'those who love her' / Q ʾōhăbay 'those who love me'); Prov 8:35 (K mṣʾy 'those who find me' / Q māṣāʾ 'has found').
entries.rationale: The Leningrad Codex marks each Ketiv/Qere pair, and the source edition prints the Ketiv consonants followed by the vocalized Qere in brackets. The Masoretic reading tradition reads the Qere, and English translations, including the ASV baseline, follow it in nearly every case (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012). This is the corpus baseline (genesis-woh; exodus-woh; ketiv-qere-qere-translated-kings; ketiv-qere-qere-translated-ezekiel; job-woh 38:1 and 42), made explicit here for the four Writings books. Two of the six pairs change the English: at Ps 139:16 the ASV ('when as yet there was none of them') follows the Ketiv, and the Qere gives 'and for it there was one among them'; at Ps 147:19 the Ketiv and the ASV have the singular 'word', the Qere the plural 'words'. In both cases the line follows the Qere, and the commentary gives the Ketiv and the ASV. The other pairs are orthographic (Ps 139:6), a difference of number rendered collectively (Job 37:12), or restore the first-person speech the context needs (Prov 8:17, 35).

entries.translit: MT ; superscription as v 1 ; petuḥa / setuma
entries.lemma: the Masoretic consonants, vocalization, verse numbering and paragraph marks where the ancient versions (LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate, Targum) or modern emendations read otherwise
entries.standardEnglish: the ASV follows the MT at most of these sites; NRSV adopts the versional or emended reading at Ps 19:5; 33:7; 139:11, 18; Prov 8:16; 10:10; Eccl 3:21
entries.wohChoice: Translate the Masoretic Text and give the versional or conjectural reading in commentary. Follow the Masoretic verse numbering, which in the Psalms counts a superscription as v 1 (Ps 8:1; 19:1) or runs it into v 1 (Ps 139:1), so that MT Ps 8:6 = ASV 8:5 and MT Ps 19:15 = ASV 19:14. Keep the Masoretic paragraph marks (פ / ס) in the Hebrew text with no English marker. Wave W1 sites: Ps 8:3 'strength' (LXX 'praise'); 19:5 'their line' (LXX 'sound') and 'in them' (emended 'in the sea'); 33:7 'as a heap' (LXX 'as a wineskin'); 139:11 'overwhelm' (emended 'cover'); 139:14 'I am ... made' (LXX 'you are'); 139:18 'I awake' (emended 'I come to the end'); 147:1 the MT psalm unit (LXX and Vulgate Pss 146-147); 147:20 'they have not known them' (LXX 'he did not make known'); Job 37:7 'all the men of his making'; 37:13 'for his land'; Prov 8:16 'all who judge righteously' (variant 'the judges of the earth'); 10:10 the repeated half-line (LXX different); Eccl 3:17 'there' (emended 'he has appointed'); 3:21 the articular participles 'that goes upward ... that goes downward' (LXX, Vulgate, ASV 'whether'; the KJV follows the MT pointing). One exception, in the vowels only: at Ps 8:2 the MT imperative tĕnâ does not construe after ʾăšer, and the line reads the same consonants as a perfect ('you who have set', ASV, NRSV), recording the MT form. Words are supplied only where English needs them to construe the Hebrew (Ps 139:20 'your name', with the ASV).
entries.rationale: The corpus translates the MT and records versional readings instead of adopting them (mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-and-versification-kings; mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-ezekiel; mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah). The policy keeps the translation predictable and makes the apparatus, not the line, the place where the textual evidence is weighed (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012). Two applications in this wave go against most modern versions and are named for the Reviewer. At Eccl 3:21 the Masoretic vowels give both participles the article, so that the verse asks who knows the breath 'that goes upward'; the LXX, the Vulgate, the ASV, NRSV and NJPS read the interrogative ('whether it goes upward'), which the same consonants allow (the KJV, 'the spirit of man that goeth upward', follows the MT pointing), and many commentators take the Masoretic pointing as a later theological smoothing. The line keeps the MT, and the commentary sets out the alternative. At Prov 8:16 the Leningrad reading ṣedeq is kept against the many manuscripts and versions that read ʾāreṣ. At Ps 8:2, by contrast, the MT vowels give an imperative that has no syntax after the relative ʾăšer; there the line reads the unchanged consonants as the ASV and NRSV do, and the commentary records the Masoretic form. The Psalms follow the MT numbering because the canon cites them in the MT numbering of the French Bibles ('Psaumes VIII-6', 'XIX-7'), which is also the numbering of the refIds; the ASV numbers are given in commentary where they differ.

entries.partOfSpeech: convention: English lineation, superscriptions and speech marking in the poetic books
entries.wohChoice: One English line per Masoretic verse. The parallel halves of a verse stay in one line, divided by a semicolon or comma at the main disjunctive accent (ʾatnaḥ, or ʿôlê wĕyôrēd in the poetic accentuation of Job, Psalms and Proverbs), with no indentation or line breaks. Speeches that fill a chapter (Elihu, Job 37; Wisdom, Prov 8:4-36) have no outer quotation marks, as in job-woh 38-41; embedded direct speech takes double quotation marks (Job 37:6); internal speech after 'I said in my heart' is introduced with a colon and no quotation marks (Eccl 3:17-18, ASV practice). Psalm superscriptions are translated within the verse that carries them. Personified wisdom is lower case (chokhmah-personified-wisdom-proverbs).
entries.rationale: The library reader shows one English string per refId, aligned with the Hebrew verse, so the structure of Hebrew poetry has to be shown inside the line. The Masoretic accents mark the main division of each poetic verse, and punctuating at that division shows the parallelism without inventing a lineation the source does not mark (on the poetic accents, Yeivin, Introduction to the Tiberian Masorah, 1980). The quotation-mark practice follows the signed-off job-woh chapters 38-41, where YHWH's speeches run without outer quotation marks and embedded speech is marked, and the double-quotation-mark convention of the Kings and Ezekiel overlays for embedded speech. Internal speech in Ecclesiastes is reflection, not dialogue; the ASV introduces it with a colon, and the convention keeps that, so that the reader does not take Qohelet's thought for a quoted saying.

entries.lemma: technical terms of the Psalm superscriptions
entries.partOfSpeech: participle with preposition; noun; preposition + noun (superscription formulas)
entries.literal: to/for the director; a song with accompaniment of/for David; upon the Gittite (instrument or tune)
entries.standardEnglish: For the Chief Musician; A Psalm of David; set to the Gittith (ASV); To the leader (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'For the Chief Musician' (lamnaṣṣēaḥ), 'A Psalm of David' (mizmôr lĕdāwid, lĕdāwid mizmôr), 'set to the Gittith' (ʿal-haggittît), with the ASV; the superscription is translated as part of the verse that carries it (MT v 1).
entries.rationale: The superscriptions use musical and liturgical terms whose meaning was partly lost by the time of the Greek translation. lamnaṣṣēaḥ is the Piel participle of nṣḥ 'direct, oversee' with the preposition lĕ- (BDB; HALOT): 'for the leader' or 'to the choirmaster'; the LXX eis to telos 'for the end' shows that the sense was already uncertain. mizmôr is a song sung with instrumental accompaniment (from zmr 'sing, play'). ʿal-haggittît (Pss 8, 81, 84) names an instrument or melody connected with Gath or with the winepress (gat; LXX 'over the winepresses'); 'Gittith' keeps the term without guessing. lĕdāwid can mean 'by David', 'for David' or 'belonging to the David collection' (Craigie, Psalms 1-50, WBC 19, 1983; Kraus, Psalms 1-59, 1988), and English 'of David' keeps the ambiguity. The ASV wording is accurate for these terms and is kept.

entries.source: תּוֹרַת / עֵדוּת / פִּקּוּדֵי / מִצְוַת / יִרְאַת / מִשְׁפְּטֵי יְהוָה
entries.translit: tôrat / ʿēdût / piqqûdê / miṣwat / yirʾat / mišpĕṭê YHWH
entries.lemma: the six Torah terms of Ps 19:8-10
entries.literal: instruction / testimony / precepts / command / fear / judgments of YHWH
entries.standardEnglish: law / testimony / precepts / commandment / fear / ordinances (ASV); teaching / decrees / precepts / instruction / fear / judgments (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'the law of YHWH', 'the testimony of YHWH', 'the precepts of YHWH', 'the commandment of YHWH', 'the fear of YHWH', 'the ordinances of YHWH' (ASV), one English word for each Hebrew term (Ps 19:8-10).
entries.rationale: Ps 19:8-10 names YHWH's instruction six times with six different terms, a series that Ps 119 develops at length (Kraus, Psalms 1-59; Craigie, WBC 19). Each term keeps its own English word so that the series stays visible. tôrâ is rendered 'law' here, as in the Kings overlay (torah-law-deuteronomistic-kings), because in this psalm it heads a series of legal terms (testimony, precepts, commandment, ordinances) and names a fixed body of instruction that 'restores' and 'makes wise'. The isaiah-woh overlay's 'teaching' (torah-teaching-isaiah) answers a prophetic usage in which tôrâ is the present instruction of a prophet or of YHWH; the two renderings are register decisions to be reconciled by a later corpus-wide entry. yirʾat YHWH 'the fear of YHWH' stands in the series for the instruction that produces reverence; the emendation ʾimrat 'the word of' has no textual support and is not adopted. mišpāṭîm is 'ordinances', as in Ps 147:19-20 in this wave and in the ASV.

entries.literal: you wove me, you knit me together
entries.standardEnglish: thou didst cover me (ASV; KJV 'thou hast covered me'); you knit me together (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'you knit me together in my mother's womb' (Ps 139:13)
entries.rationale: Hebrew has two roots skk: I 'screen, cover' (Ex 25:20; 1 Kgs 8:7) and II 'weave, knit together'. BDB and HALOT place Ps 139:13 with Job 10:11 ('with bones and sinews you knit me together', tĕsōkĕkēnî) under skk II. The context supports it: in v 15 the psalmist was 'intricately wrought' (ruqqamtî, from rqm 'weave in colors') in secret. The ASV and KJV 'covered' follow skk I; NRSV and most modern versions have 'knit me together'. The lexical consensus is followed, as job-woh did at Job 42:10 where the critical consensus on a derivation is settled. The rendering carries no lens: it states the Hebrew image of the forming of the embryo as weaving, which recurs at Job 10:11 and, on one derivation, at Prov 8:23 nissaktî (recorded there, not adopted).
